paragraphs: More people are buying their first home in Ireland. New numbers show this.
From July to September, 8,164 first-time buyers got a mortgage. A mortgage is a loan to buy a home. This is the highest number for these months since 2008.

In total, people took out 14,217 mortgages in these three months. They were worth €4.6 billion. First-time buyers got almost six in ten of them. The number of people moving their mortgage to a new bank also went up a lot.
Government schemes, like Help to Buy, give money to these buyers. But homes are still too expensive for many couples near Dublin.
More first-time buyers got mortgages in the summer months than at any time since 2008, new figures show.
According to Banking and Payments Federation Ireland (BPFI), 8,164 first-time buyers took out a mortgage between July and September. Of these, 3,244 were for new homes, up 7.5% on last year.

In total, 14,217 mortgages worth €4.6 billion were drawn down in the three months. That is 13% more than a year earlier. First-time buyers got almost six in every ten. The number of people switching their mortgage to another lender also rose sharply, by almost 42%.

The BPFI says three Government schemes are helping first-time buyers: Help to Buy, the First Home scheme and the Local Authority Home Loan. Its chief executive, Brian Hayes, said the market was growing in every area.
However, buying a home is still hard for many people. A study earlier this year found that a couple earning €113,000 together could still be about €25,000 short of the price of a home in Kildare.
First-time buyers drew down more mortgages in the third quarter than in any comparable period since 2008, according to new figures from Banking and Payments Federation Ireland (BPFI).

Some 8,164 first-time buyer mortgages were issued between July and September. Of these, 3,244 were for newly built homes, a rise of 7.5% on the same period last year, while the number of self-build loans fell by 5.8%.

Across the whole market, 14,217 mortgages worth €4.6 billion were drawn down, an increase of 13% in volume and almost 16% in value. First-time buyers made up 57% of the total, and remortgaging and switching jumped by almost 42%.

The BPFI said demand was being driven partly by State schemes such as Help to Buy, the First Home scheme and the Local Authority Home Loan. Chief executive Brian Hayes said the figures showed continued momentum, with growth in every segment.

Affordability remains a concern, however. A study published in July by the Society of Chartered Surveyors Ireland found that a couple on a combined income of €113,000 with a 10% deposit would still face a gap of almost €25,000 in Kildare, €20,500 in Wicklow and €11,500 in Meath.

Affordability nonetheless remains a sticking point. Research published in July by the Society of Chartered Surveyors Ireland estimated that a dual-income couple earning €113,000 with a 10% deposit would still confront a shortfall of almost €25,000 in Kildare, €20,500 in Wicklow and €11,500 in Meath.
